worksheet.title: Two Scripts, One Event
worksheet.subtitle: The same event starts both scripts
worksheet.learning_goal: I can read two scripts that the same event starts at the same time.

parts.title: One event, two scripts
parts.text: Bit (green) and Pixel (purple) each have their own script. Look at the top of each one — they BOTH start with 'when green flag clicked'. So ONE click of the green flag starts BOTH scripts at the SAME time. Two scripts running together are called parallel scripts. Each sprite moves from its own home.

parts.title: Where does Bit land?
parts.prompt: The green flag is clicked. Bit's script runs from home 0: forward 2. What number does Bit land on?

parts.title: Where does Pixel land?
parts.prompt: The same green flag also starts Pixel's script from home 5: back 1. What number does Pixel land on?

parts.title: One event, both at once
parts.prompt: How many times did you click the green flag to start BOTH scripts? Write the number. Then write where each lands. Bit: ____  Pixel: ____

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: When two scripts share the same event hat, ONE event starts them both — they run in parallel. You only click the green flag once, and both Bit and Pixel go at the same time, each on its own script.

teacher_guide.title: Two Scripts, One Event
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key
teacher_guide.footer_topic: 2. Two Scripts, One Event — Teacher Guide

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students see that one event can start more than one set of moves: the same "when green flag clicked" hat sits on top of both Bit's and Pixel's moves, so one click starts BOTH at the same time. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer needed — paper and a pencil. You read the prompts aloud. Optional: two counters on a number line 0 to 5 (green Bit, purple Pixel), and a card that says "go" you can hand over to act out sending a message.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). One green-flag click; both Bit and Pixel start because both have the green-flag hat.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Bit lands on 2; Exercise 2 — Pixel lands on 4.
3. Let them try. Students count the clicks needed (one) and write both landings (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Bit: 0, forward 2 → 2. Exercise 2 — Pixel: 5, back 1 → 4.
Exercise 3 — ONE green-flag click starts both (the same event sits on top of both). Bit lands on 2, Pixel on 4.
Key idea: one event can trigger two sets of moves, so they run at the same time from that single click.

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: thinking each set needs its own click. One matching event starts both.
Make it easier: click once, then move the green and purple counters.
Make it harder: ask what would happen if only one set had the green-flag hat.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events.
In plain terms: students write and run instructions that are started by an event, like clicking the green flag or getting a message.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential and concurrent events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read instructions, change what starts them or one move, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child sees one click start both sets of moves and writes both landings.
